title: Principles of microeconomics
summary: A first course in how individuals, firms and governments make choices under scarcity. Students use tables of numbers and graphs every week to study markets, elasticity, consumer choice, firm costs, competition and monopoly, and market failure. The course follows OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e.
brief: Principles of microeconomics for first-year undergraduates: a six-week summer session, each week a two-hour lecture and a one-hour problem section. Textbook: OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e. Week by week: 1, scarcity, choice and opportunity cost, and the production possibilities frontier; 2, demand, supply and market equilibrium, and what shifts each curve; 3, elasticity and its uses (taxes, total revenue); 4, consumer choice and the costs of a firm in the short and long run; 5, perfect competition and monopoly; 6, externalities, public goods and what governments do about them. Students work with tables of numbers and graphs every week. Weekly problem sets 30% (due before the next lecture), a midterm exam in week 3 (30%), a final exam at the end of week 6 (40%).
policies:
Problem sets are submitted online before the next lecture; a late set loses 10% a day and is not accepted after the answers are posted.

A calculator is allowed on both exams; a phone is not. Bring a ruler and pencil to every problem section for graphs.

The teacher defines scarcity, the factors of production (land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship), trade-off and opportunity cost.
The teacher introduces a hypothetical student, Maya, with an 8-hour Saturday.
Before any answer is given, every student writes Maya’s opportunity cost of studying, then compares with a partner.
The teacher then states the answer and shows that the cost is the single best alternative given up, not a list of all alternatives.

segments.title: Reading a production possibilities table
segments.description:
The teacher introduces a hypothetical economy, Zeda, that makes only wheat and cloth, and shows its table of production choices.
In pairs, students calculate what is given up in cloth when Zeda moves from A to B, then from B to C.
The teacher shows the method on the board: opportunity cost is the change in cloth for each extra million tons of wheat.
Students then finish the last two steps themselves and check against the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 2, 6, 12 and 20 thousand bolts per million tons of wheat, for A to B through D to E. Common mistake: reading the cloth level at the new point (92) as the cost. Cost is the difference between rows.

segments.title: Draw a frontier from data
segments.description:
Students receive a new table for a hypothetical island economy that produces fish and coconuts.
Working alone with a ruler and pencil, they draw and label axes, plot the six points, and join them with a smooth curve.
Then they calculate the opportunity cost of each step and mark which step costs the most.
The teacher circulates and checks axes, labels and units.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: costs of 3, 7, 12, 18 and 20 thousand coconuts per ton of fish, the last step costing most. Check that axes match their labels and units. A smooth curve is illustrative; straight segments connecting adjacent points also represent the table. Without graph paper, use the ruler to mark equal spacing for each unit.

segments.title: Break
segments.description:

segments.title: Why the frontier bows outward
segments.description:
Students look at Zeda’s costs of 2, 6, 12 and 20 and write whether the next million tons of wheat would cost more or less than 20 thousand bolts if increasing opportunity cost continues, and what that means for the shape of the curve.
The teacher compares a straight-line frontier with a bowed-out one.
The teacher explains the reason: the first resources moved are the best suited to the new good, and later ones are less suited.
Students explain the reason to a partner using Zeda’s land and workers.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected answer: if increasing opportunity cost continues, the next million tons costs more than 20 thousand bolts. With wheat on the horizontal axis, the frontier becomes steeper. Example: land that grows wheat well moves first. Later, hill pasture and mill workers are moved, and they are poor at wheat. Mistake: blaming tired workers or higher prices.

segments.title: Efficiency, unattainable points and growth
segments.description:
Students decide which of three Zeda points are attainable and which are efficient, and write a reason for each.
The teacher marks the points on the board and explains that points inside the frontier waste resources, while points outside cannot be reached with present resources and technology.
The teacher then draws an outward shift of the wheat end of the frontier from a better seed.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: (3, 70) attainable but inefficient, as 10 thousand more bolts are possible without reducing wheat production; (3, 80) attainable and efficient, it is point D; (3, 90) unattainable. A shift of the frontier is growth, not a move along it.

segments.title: Find and fix the mistake
segments.description:
Students receive three statements about Zeda that each contain one error.
Working alone for five minutes, they find the error in each and write a corrected version.
Students compare with a partner, then the teacher hears a correction for each statement.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. ‘Moving from C to D costs 80 thousand bolts, the cloth left at D.’ Fix: the cost is the change, 92 − 80 = 12 thousand bolts.
2. ‘The frontier bows out because wheat workers get tired.’ Fix: resources are not equally suited to both goods, so costs rise.
3. ‘Producing 3 million tons of wheat with 70 thousand bolts is impossible because it is off the frontier.’ Fix: it is attainable but inefficient, inside the frontier.

segments.title: Which point on the frontier?
segments.description:
Pairs write which Zeda point from A to E they would choose and what else they would want to know.
The teacher hears from three pairs and asks the class to respond to each choice.
The teacher closes by noting that every point on the frontier is efficient, but the frontier cannot say which point is best.
segments.teacherNotes: Draw out that choosing among efficient points needs values and information about who gains or loses. Economists separate what is possible from what is desirable. Let students disagree.

segments.title: Individual check
segments.description:
Students work alone for five minutes on a new table for a hypothetical firm making desks and chairs.
The teacher then goes over the answers for two minutes.
Students mark their own work and note anything to ask about.
segments.teacherNotes:
Table: desks 0, 10, 20, 30 with chairs 60, 56, 46, 30.

Q2. Is 20 desks and 40 chairs attainable, and efficient? Answer: attainable, not efficient, since 46 is possible.

keyIdeas: Scarcity means limited resources against unlimited wants, so every choice involves a trade-off.

study.overview: Every economy, firm and person has limited resources and many wants, so every choice gives something up. This guide covers the cost of a choice, how to calculate it from a table of production choices, how a production possibilities frontier (PPF) shows what an economy can and cannot produce, and why the frontier usually bows outward. The examples are the hypothetical economy of Zeda, which makes only wheat and cloth, and Maya, a student with a free Saturday. For more reading, see the OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, chapter Choice in a World of Scarcity.

points.heading: Scarcity, trade-offs and opportunity cost
points.explanation:
Scarcity means limited resources set against unlimited wants. Resources are the factors of production: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship. Because they are limited, choosing one use means giving up others. That is a trade-off.

The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative given up. It is one alternative, not the whole list.

Example: Suppose Maya has an 8-hour Saturday. She can work a shift at the campus café for $15 an hour, or she can study for Monday’s quiz. If the shift is her best alternative, the opportunity cost of studying is 8 × $15 = $120. Two mistakes to avoid. Do not add up every alternative she could have chosen. Do not count a tuition or textbook price as the cost of this Saturday, because that money is spent whichever way she uses the day. Time and money are both scarce, and the cost of a choice can be measured in either.

points.heading: Calculating opportunity cost from a table
points.explanation:
A table of production choices lists combinations of two goods that an economy can make. The opportunity cost of moving from one row to the next is the change in the good given up, divided by the change in the good gained.

Zeda’s table:
A: 0 million tons of wheat, 100 thousand bolts of cloth
B: 1 million tons of wheat, 98 thousand bolts of cloth
C: 2 million tons of wheat, 92 thousand bolts of cloth
D: 3 million tons of wheat, 80 thousand bolts of cloth
E: 4 million tons of wheat, 60 thousand bolts of cloth

From A to B, wheat rises by 1 million tons and cloth falls from 100 to 98. The cost is 2 thousand bolts per million tons of wheat. The same method gives 6 for B to C, 12 for C to D and 20 for D to E.

The common error is to read the cloth level at the new point, such as 92, as the cost. The cost is the difference between rows. If a step covers more than one unit of the gained good, divide by that change. Moving from B to D, cloth falls by 98 − 80 = 18 thousand bolts while wheat rises by 2 million tons. The cost is 18 ÷ 2 = 9 thousand bolts per million tons of wheat, an average over the two steps.

points.heading: Reading a production possibilities frontier
points.explanation:
A PPF shows the most of two goods an economy can produce with its present resources and technology. To draw one, put one good on each axis, label the units, space the units equally, plot every point from the table and join adjacent points. A smooth curve is an illustration. Straight segments between the points also represent the table.

The frontier divides all combinations into three kinds:
• On the frontier: efficient. No more of one good can be made without making less of the other.
• Inside the frontier: attainable but inefficient. Resources are wasted or unused.
• Outside the frontier: unattainable with present resources and technology.

Example with Zeda’s table, taking 2 million tons of wheat. Point C is on the frontier at 92 thousand bolts, so it is efficient. Producing 85 thousand bolts is attainable but inefficient, because 7 thousand more bolts could be made without losing any wheat. Producing 95 thousand bolts is unattainable.

Suppose a better wheat seed lets Zeda grow more wheat from the same land. The wheat end of the frontier shifts outward. That is economic growth, a shift of the whole frontier. It is not a move along the frontier from one point to another.

Every point on the frontier is efficient, but the frontier cannot say which point is best. That choice depends on values and on who gains or loses, which is why economists separate what is possible from what is desirable.

points.heading: Why the frontier bows outward
points.explanation:
Zeda’s opportunity costs rise at every step: 2, 6, 12 and then 20 thousand bolts per million tons of wheat. This is increasing opportunity cost. With wheat on the horizontal axis, it makes the frontier steeper as wheat output grows, so the curve bows outward. If the pattern continues, the next million tons of wheat costs more than 20 thousand bolts.

The reason is that resources are not equally well suited to making both goods. The first resources moved to wheat are the best suited to it. Land that grows wheat well moves first. Later, Zeda must move hill pasture and mill workers, who are poor at growing wheat. Each extra million tons then takes more cloth production with it.

Compare a straight-line frontier. Its opportunity cost is constant, which would hold only if resources were equally suited to both goods.

Do not explain the bow by saying that workers get tired, or that prices rise. The cause is differences in how well resources suit each good.

Opportunity cost table:
A to B: (100 − 97) ÷ (1 − 0) = 3 thousand coconuts per ton of fish.
B to C: (97 − 90) ÷ (2 − 1) = 7 thousand coconuts per ton of fish.
C to D: (90 − 78) ÷ (3 − 2) = 12 thousand coconuts per ton of fish.
D to E: (78 − 60) ÷ (4 − 3) = 18 thousand coconuts per ton of fish.
E to F: (60 − 40) ÷ (5 − 4) = 20 thousand coconuts per ton of fish.
Which step costs the most? E to F should be circled and written in the blank. It costs 20 thousand coconuts for the additional ton of fish. Common slip: reporting coconuts remaining instead of coconuts forgone.

handouts.key:
Statement 1: The error is treating the cloth remaining at D as the opportunity cost. Corrected statement: Moving from C to D costs 92 − 80 = 12 thousand bolts of cloth for 1 additional million tons of wheat.
Statement 2: The error is attributing the bowed-out frontier to worker fatigue. Corrected statement: The frontier bows outward because resources are not equally suited to producing wheat and cloth. As wheat production expands, resources increasingly valuable in cloth production move into wheat production, so more cloth is forgone per additional million tons of wheat. Common slip: attributing the shape to changes in prices.
Statement 3: The error is treating every point off the frontier as impossible. Corrected statement: Producing 3 million tons of wheat and 70 thousand bolts of cloth is attainable but productively inefficient. At the same wheat output, D provides 80 thousand bolts, so 80 − 70 = 10 thousand additional bolts are possible. Common slip: confusing points inside the frontier with points outside it.

Which point, and why? Accept any point A through E with a reason that recognizes its trade-off. A provides 100 thousand bolts of cloth and no wheat; B provides 98 thousand bolts and 1 million tons of wheat; C provides 92 thousand bolts and 2 million tons of wheat; D provides 80 thousand bolts and 3 million tons of wheat; E provides 60 thousand bolts and 4 million tons of wheat. All are productively efficient. Look for an argument about the relative value of wheat and cloth, rather than a claim that one point is uniquely efficient.
What else would you want to know? Look for information about people's preferences, food and clothing needs, population, existing stocks, and how output is distributed. Strong answers explain how that information could change the choice. Common slip: assuming the frontier alone identifies the most desirable production mix.

handouts.title: Individual check

blocks.text: A hypothetical firm makes only desks and chairs. Work alone for five minutes. Its table of production choices is below.

items: What is the opportunity cost of the second 10 desks?
Is 20 desks and 40 chairs attainable? Is it efficient? Give a reason.
Does opportunity cost rise as the firm makes more desks? Show your working.

blocks.hint: After the answers are gone over, note anything you want to ask about.

handouts.key:
Opportunity cost of the second 10 desks: Increasing desk production from 10 to 20 reduces chair production from 56 to 46. Opportunity cost = 56 − 46 = 10 chairs. Common slip: using the 46 chairs remaining or calculating the cost of the first 20 desks.
Is 20 desks and 40 chairs attainable and efficient? It is attainable but productively inefficient. The table allows 46 chairs at 20 desks, so 46 − 40 = 6 additional chairs could be produced without reducing desk output.
Does opportunity cost rise? Yes. From 0 to 10 desks: 60 − 56 = 4 chairs. From 10 to 20 desks: 56 − 46 = 10 chairs. From 20 to 30 desks: 46 − 30 = 16 chairs. These costs rise for equal increments of 10 desks. Equivalently, the costs per desk are 0.4, 1, and 1.6 chairs. Common slip: comparing total chair output instead of the chairs forgone at each step.
Anything to ask about: Answers vary. Accept a specific question about the calculations, attainability, efficiency, or increasing opportunity cost, or a statement that no questions remain.

keyIdeas: With everything else held equal, buyers want less as the price rises and sellers offer more. A demand curve therefore slopes down and a supply curve slopes up, and both can be plotted from a price and quantity table.
Equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Above it there is a surplus and the price tends to fall. Below it there is a shortage and the price tends to rise.
A change in the good’s own price moves us along a curve. A change in another determinant of demand or supply, such as income or input costs, shifts the relevant curve.

A rise in demand raises both the equilibrium price and quantity. A rise in supply lowers the price and raises the quantity. When both curves move, one of the two effects is certain and the other depends on the sizes of the shifts.

vocabulary.definition: Latin for ‘other things being equal’: the habit of changing one factor in an analysis while holding all others fixed.
When the price of a good rises and nothing else changes, the quantity demanded falls, so the demand curve slopes down.
When the price of a good rises and nothing else changes, the quantity supplied rises, so the supply curve slopes up.
The price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, where the demand and supply curves cross.
The amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a price below equilibrium.
The amount by which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a price above equilibrium.
A change in demand or supply at every price, caused by a change in another determinant of demand or supply, such as income or input costs.
A good for which demand rises when consumers’ incomes rise, and falls when incomes fall.

study.overview: This guide covers how a market is read from a table of numbers. Starting from a price and quantity table for a hypothetical college town’s daily iced-coffee market, you plotted a demand curve and a supply curve, found the price where they cross, and measured shortages and surpluses at other prices. You then asked what moves the curves themselves, and what happens when two curves move in the same month. Keep your ruler graph of the town market nearby as you read. The matching reading is OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, the chapter on demand and supply.

points.heading: Turning a schedule into two curves
points.explanation:
A demand schedule lists the quantity demanded at each price, with everything else held equal (ceteris paribus). The law of demand says that as the price rises, the quantity demanded falls. The law of supply says that as the price rises, the quantity supplied rises. Quantity demanded is one number at one price. Demand is the whole schedule or curve.

The town’s iced-coffee market, in cups per day:
Price $2: demanded 140, supplied 20.
Price $3: demanded 110, supplied 50.
Price $4: demanded 80, supplied 80.
Price $5: demanded 50, supplied 110.
Price $6: demanded 20, supplied 140.

To plot it, put price in dollars on the vertical axis and quantity in cups per day on the horizontal axis. Mark the five demand points and join them with a ruler. This is D, and it slopes down. Mark the five supply points and join them. This is S, and it slopes up. These points lie on straight lines, so do not join them in a zigzag. Label both axes with units and label both curves.

points.heading: Equilibrium, shortage and surplus
points.explanation:
Equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. On your graph it is where D and S cross. In the town market that is $4 and 80 cups per day.

At any other price, read the two quantities off the curves and take the horizontal gap between them. This is a distance along the quantity axis, not along the price axis.
At $3, buyers want 110 and cafés offer 50. That is a shortage of 60 cups, not 110. Competing buyers bid the price up.
At $5, buyers want 50 and cafés offer 110. That is a surplus of 60 cups. Cafés with unsold cups cut the price.
At $2 there is a shortage of 120 (140 wanted, 20 offered). At $6 there is a surplus of 120 (20 wanted, 140 offered).
At $4, 80 and 80 means neither a shortage nor a surplus, so the price has no pressure to change.

Check: a shortage appears when the price is below equilibrium, and a surplus when it is above.

points.heading: Movement along a curve versus a shift of a curve
points.explanation:
A change in the good’s own price moves you along a curve. A change in any other determinant moves the whole curve. Demand shifters include income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations and the number of buyers. Supply shifters include input costs, technology, taxes and subsidies, the number of sellers and weather. A normal good is one whose demand rises when income rises.

Use four steps: draw the baseline market, decide which curve the event shifts, decide which way, then read the new price and quantity.

Example 1. Town incomes rise and iced coffee is a normal good. Demand shifts right by 60 cups at every price, giving 200, 170, 140, 110 and 80 cups at $2 through $6. Supply is unchanged. The new equilibrium is $5 and 110 cups, so price and quantity both rise. The rise in quantity supplied is a move along S, not a shift of supply.

Example 2. Coffee beans get cheaper, which lowers the cafés’ costs. Supply shifts right by 60 cups at every price, giving 80, 110, 140, 170 and 200 cups at $2 through $6. Demand is unchanged. The new equilibrium is $3 and 110 cups, so price falls and quantity rises. At the old price of $4 there would now be a surplus of 60 cups.

Working backwards: if the price rose and the quantity sold fell, and only one curve shifted, the shift must be supply to the left. A rise in demand alone would raise the quantity. Higher bean costs could explain a leftward shift of supply.

points.heading: When both curves move at once
points.explanation:
Suppose incomes rise and beans get cheaper in the same month. Use the two shifted columns from the town market:
Price $2: demanded 200, supplied 80.
Price $3: demanded 170, supplied 110.
Price $4: demanded 140, supplied 140.
Price $5: demanded 110, supplied 170.
Price $6: demanded 80, supplied 200.

The columns match at $4 and 140 cups. Compared with the original $4 and 80 cups, the price is unchanged and the quantity has risen.

The general rule is that when both curves shift right, quantity rises for certain. The rise in demand pushes the price up and the rise in supply pushes it down, so the price effect depends on which shift is larger. Here the two shifts are equal in size, so the price stays at $4. If the supply shift were larger than the demand shift, the price would fall. Do not assume the price rises just because demand rose. Always ask what the other curve is doing.

keyIdeas: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. The midpoint formula uses averages as the base, so the answer is the same whichever direction the price moves.
Demand is elastic when the elasticity is above 1, inelastic when it is below 1, and unit elastic when it equals 1. The absolute value is used, since the law of demand makes the raw number negative.
When price rises, total revenue (price × quantity) rises if demand is inelastic and falls if demand is elastic. A price cut does the opposite.
A tax is split between buyers and sellers according to elasticity. The side that responds less to price, and so can walk away less easily, bears more of the tax.

vocabulary.definition: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price, used as a measure of how responsive buyers are to price.
A way to find percentage changes using the average of the starting and ending values as the base, so the elasticity is the same in either direction.
Demand with an elasticity above 1, where quantity demanded changes by a larger percent than price.
Demand with an elasticity below 1, where quantity demanded changes by a smaller percent than price.
Demand with an elasticity equal to 1, where quantity demanded and price change by the same percent.
The price of a good multiplied by the quantity sold.
The way the burden of a tax is divided between buyers and sellers.

study.overview: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly buyers respond to a price change. This guide uses the iced-coffee demand schedule from the town’s cafés, with quantity in combined cups per day: $2 → 140, $3 → 110, $4 → 80, $5 → 50, $6 → 20. You will calculate elasticity with the midpoint formula, classify demand as elastic or inelastic, predict what happens to total revenue, and see how elasticity decides who bears a tax. For more practice, read the elasticity chapter of OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e.

points.heading: Calculating elasticity with the midpoint formula
points.explanation:
Price elasticity of demand = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP. The midpoint formula uses the average of the old and new values as the base for each percentage: %ΔQ = (Q₂ − Q₁) ÷ ((Q₁ + Q₂) ÷ 2) × 100, and %ΔP = (P₂ − P₁) ÷ ((P₁ + P₂) ÷ 2) × 100. A start-value base gives a different answer for each direction of the same change. The average base does not.

Example, $4 to $5. Quantity falls from 80 to 50, so ΔQ = −30 and the average quantity is 65. %ΔQ = −30 ÷ 65 ≈ −46.2%. Price rises by $1 and the average price is $4.50, so %ΔP = 1 ÷ 4.50 ≈ 22.2%. Elasticity = −46.2 ÷ 22.2 ≈ −2.08. Going from $5 back to $4 gives the same 2.08.

Steps: find the change, find the average, divide to get each percentage, divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage, then drop the sign. A common mistake is dividing by the starting value only. Another is leaving the minus sign in.

points.heading: Elastic, inelastic and unit elastic demand
points.explanation:
The law of demand makes the raw elasticity negative, so we use the absolute value. Demand is elastic when the value is above 1: quantity changes by a larger percentage than price. It is inelastic when the value is below 1: quantity changes by a smaller percentage. It is unit elastic when the value equals 1.

Example, $4 to $5: 2.08 is above 1, so demand is elastic. Now take $2 to $3. ΔQ = −30 and the average quantity is 125, so %ΔQ = −24%. ΔP = 1 and the average price is $2.50, so %ΔP = 40%. Elasticity = 24 ÷ 40 = 0.6, which is inelastic.

Elasticity is not one fixed number for a whole straight-line demand curve. On this schedule, $2 to $3 is inelastic, while $5 to $6 is elastic. Always say which interval you measured.

points.heading: Elasticity and total revenue
points.explanation:
Total revenue = price × quantity. Whether a price change raises or lowers revenue depends on elasticity.

If demand is inelastic (below 1), a price rise increases revenue and a price cut decreases it. If demand is elastic (above 1), a price rise decreases revenue and a price cut increases it. A higher price does not always mean more revenue, because quantity falls too.

Example with the coffee schedule. Revenue is $2 × 140 = $280, $3 × 110 = $330, and $4 × 80 = $320. From $2 to $3, demand is inelastic (0.6), so revenue rises from $280 to $330. From $3 to $4, the midpoint elasticity is (30 ÷ 95) ÷ (1 ÷ 3.50) ≈ 1.11, which is elastic, so revenue falls from $330 to $320. A cut from $4 to $3 reverses that move, and revenue rises from $320 to $330.

points.heading: How elasticity splits a tax
points.explanation:
Tax incidence describes who actually bears a tax. The law does not settle it. Who the government collects the tax from does not fix who pays. What matters is how easily each side can walk away. The side that responds less to price bears more of the tax.

Suppose a market has an equilibrium price of $10 and the government puts a $1 tax on each unit. The numbers below are hypothetical.

Case A: demand is inelastic and supply is elastic. Buyers pay $10.80 and sellers keep $9.80. Buyers bear $0.80 of the tax and sellers bear $0.20.

Case B: demand is elastic and supply is inelastic. Buyers pay $10.20 and sellers keep $9.20. Buyers bear $0.20 and sellers bear $0.80.

In each case the two shares add up to the $1 tax. To find a share, compare the price each side faces with the original $10.

blocks.text: Work alone, with a calculator if you have one. The table is the demand schedule for iced coffee in the town's cafés. Quantity is combined cups per day. For each price change below, find the price elasticity of demand with the midpoint formula, drop the sign, and label the result elastic or inelastic. Show your working.

blocks.text: Midpoint formula: elasticity = (change in Q ÷ average Q) ÷ (change in P ÷ average P), taken as an absolute value.
The move from $2 to $3

blocks.hint: Percent change in quantity, percent change in price, elasticity, and your label.

blocks.text: The move from $5 to $6

blocks.hint: Percent change in quantity, percent change in price, elasticity, and your label.

handouts.key:
The move from $2 to $3
Change in quantity = 110 − 140 = −30 cups per day. Average quantity = (140 + 110) ÷ 2 = 125 cups per day. Percent change in quantity = (−30 ÷ 125) × 100 = −24%.
Change in price = $3 − $2 = $1. Average price = ($2 + $3) ÷ 2 = $2.50. Percent change in price = (1 ÷ 2.50) × 100 = 40%.
Price elasticity of demand = |−24% ÷ 40%| = 0.60. Demand is inelastic because 0.60 < 1.
Look for both midpoint denominators and a positive final elasticity. Common slip: using 140 or 110 instead of 125 as the quantity denominator.

The move from $5 to $6
Change in quantity = 20 − 50 = −30 cups per day. Average quantity = (50 + 20) ÷ 2 = 35 cups per day. Percent change in quantity = (−30 ÷ 35) × 100 ≈ −85.71%.
Change in price = $6 − $5 = $1. Average price = ($5 + $6) ÷ 2 = $5.50. Percent change in price = (1 ÷ 5.50) × 100 ≈ 18.18%.
Price elasticity of demand = |(−30 ÷ 35) ÷ (1 ÷ 5.50)| = 33 ÷ 7 ≈ 4.71. Demand is elastic because 4.71 > 1.
Look for calculations using unrounded intermediate values. Common slips: using 50 as the quantity denominator or retaining the negative sign in the final elasticity.

handouts.title: Find and fix the mistake

blocks.text: Each statement below is about the iced-coffee market and contains one error. Work alone. Underline the error in each statement, then write the correction in a few words.
Statement 1
Going from $4 to $5 gives 1.5, but going from $5 to $4 gives 3, so elasticity depends on the direction.

blocks.hint: Correction

blocks.text: Statement 2
Elasticity is 0.6, so a price cut raises combined revenue.

blocks.hint: Correction

blocks.text: Statement 3
Elasticity is −2.08, below 1, so demand is inelastic.

blocks.hint: Correction

handouts.key:
Statement 1
Underline “so elasticity depends on the direction.” The values 1.5 and 3 use starting values as percentage bases. The midpoint formula gives the same absolute elasticity in both directions: |(−30 ÷ 65) ÷ (1 ÷ 4.50)| = 27 ÷ 13 ≈ 2.08. Reversing direction reverses both changes and leaves the ratio unchanged.
Look for an explanation that the percentage bases cause the difference. Common slip: treating 1.5 and 3 as midpoint elasticities.

Statement 2
Underline “raises combined revenue.” Correction: demand is inelastic, so a price cut lowers combined revenue. For the corresponding cut from $3 to $2, revenue falls from $3 × 110 = $330 per day to $2 × 140 = $280 per day.
Look for the link between inelastic demand and a quantity increase proportionately smaller than the price decrease. Common slip: assuming that selling more cups necessarily raises revenue.

Statement 3
Underline “below 1, so demand is inelastic.” Correction: use the absolute value, 2.08. Since 2.08 > 1, demand is elastic.
Look for classification by the magnitude of elasticity. Common slip: comparing the signed ratio with 1 instead of its absolute value.

keyIdeas: A consumer with a fixed budget maximizes utility by spending all of it so that marginal utility per dollar is equal across goods: MU of coffee ÷ price of coffee = MU of bagels ÷ price of bagels.
Marginal utility diminishes as more of a good is consumed. This is why buyers spread their money across goods, and why a higher price leads them to buy less.
In the short run a firm has fixed and variable costs. Marginal cost eventually rises because of diminishing marginal returns, and it cuts the average cost curves at their lowest points.
In the long run every input can change. The long-run average cost curve is the lower edge of the short-run curves for different plant sizes, and its slope shows economies or diseconomies of scale.

A cost that does not change with output in the short run, such as rent on an oven.
A cost that changes with output, such as wages for extra workers.
The change in total cost from producing one more unit: ΔTC ÷ ΔQ.
The lowest average cost of producing each output when all inputs, including plant size, can change.
A fall in long-run average cost as output rises.

study.overview: This guide covers two linked questions. How does a consumer with a fixed budget choose among goods, and how do a firm’s costs behave as output and plant size change? Both rest on marginal thinking: compare the extra benefit or extra cost of one more unit. The examples are the ones from class: a student with $24 buying iced coffee and bagels, and a small bakery with one oven. All the numbers are made up for practice.

points.heading: Choose by marginal utility per dollar, not marginal utility
points.explanation:
A student has $24. Iced coffee costs $4 and a bagel costs $2. Put coffee on the horizontal axis and bagels on the vertical axis. The budget constraint runs from 6 coffees (24 ÷ 4) to 12 bagels (24 ÷ 2). Its slope is −4 ÷ 2 = −2, so one more coffee costs two bagels. That is an opportunity cost.

Marginal utility (MU) is the extra satisfaction from one more unit. It diminishes as you consume more of a good. The made-up MU in utils is:
Coffee, units 1 to 6: 40, 32, 24, 16, 8, 4
Bagels, units 1 to 6: 22, 18, 14, 8, 6, 2

The first coffee has a higher MU than the first bagel (40 versus 22). But coffee costs twice as much, so compare MU ÷ price:
Coffee per dollar: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 1
Bagels per dollar: 11, 9, 7, 4, 3, 1

Per dollar, the first bagel (11) beats the first coffee (10). Keep buying the affordable next unit with the highest MU per dollar, choosing coffee when ratios tie. The order is bagel (11), coffee (10), bagel (9), coffee (8), bagel (7), coffee (6), coffee (4), bagel (4). Spending runs $2, $6, $8, $12, $14, $18, $22, $24. The bundle is 4 coffees and 4 bagels, with 4 utils per dollar on the last unit of each good.

Total utility is 40 + 32 + 24 + 16 = 112 from coffee plus 22 + 18 + 14 + 8 = 62 from bagels, which is 174 utils. The bundle of 3 coffees and 6 bagels also costs $24, but it gives 96 + 70 = 166 utils. Spending the whole budget is necessary but not enough. The rule is MU of coffee ÷ price of coffee = MU of bagels ÷ price of bagels. With whole units that equality may not hold exactly, so compare the feasible bundles. A common error is comparing MU without dividing by price.

points.heading: A higher price lowers the quantity bought: the law of demand
points.explanation:
Now let the price of coffee rise from $4 to $8, with $24 and bagels still $2. The MU numbers do not change, but MU per dollar for coffee must be recomputed:
Coffee per dollar at $8: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0.5
Bagels per dollar at $2: 11, 9, 7, 4, 3, 1

Buy in order of highest ratio: bagel (11), bagel (9), bagel (7), coffee (5). Then coffee and bagel tie at 4, so buy the coffee, then the bagel. The new bundle is 2 coffees and 4 bagels. Its cost is 2 × $8 + 4 × $2 = $16 + $8 = $24. Each good gives 4 utils per dollar on its last unit.

Plot price on the vertical axis and quantity of coffee on the horizontal axis. The points are (quantity 4, price $4) and (quantity 2, price $8). When the price rises, each coffee gives less MU per dollar, so the student buys fewer coffees. This is the law of demand, built from diminishing marginal utility and a budget. In this example the number of bagels stays at 4. The student gives up coffee and keeps spending the money on bagels.

points.heading: Short-run costs: marginal cost cuts the average curves at their minimums
points.explanation:
A small bakery rents one oven for $60 a day, and this fixed cost is paid even at zero output. It hires labor at $5 per labor hour, so variable cost is labor hours × $5. The formulas are TC = FC + VC, MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ, AFC = FC ÷ Q, AVC = VC ÷ Q and ATC = TC ÷ Q.

Batches per day (Q) | labor hours | VC | TC
0 | 0 | $0 | $60
1 | 8 | $40 | $100
2 | 14 | $70 | $130
3 | 18 | $90 | $150
4 | 24 | $120 | $180
5 | 33 | $165 | $225
6 | 45 | $225 | $285

From these, for Q = 1 to 6:
MC: 40, 30, 20, 30, 45, 60
AFC: 60, 30, 20, 15, 12, 10
AVC: 40, 35, 30, 30, 33, 37.5
ATC: 100, 65, 50, 45, 45, 47.5

MC falls at first because workers specialize. It then rises because of diminishing marginal returns: the oven is fixed, so each added worker adds less output and more hours are needed per batch (6, then 9, then 12 after the third batch). MC is the change in total cost, so do not divide it by Q.

MC cuts the averages at their lowest points. ATC reaches its minimum of $45 at Q = 4 and Q = 5, and MC equals ATC at Q = 5. AVC has a minimum of $30 at Q = 3 and Q = 4, and MC equals AVC at Q = 4. The rule is that MC below an average pulls it down, and MC above an average pulls it up. ATC is U-shaped because AFC keeps falling while AVC eventually rises. At Q = 4, ATC = AFC + AVC = $15 + $30 = $45.

points.heading: Long-run average cost and economies of scale
points.explanation:
In the long run every input can change, including plant size. Each plant size has its own short-run ATC curve. The long-run average cost (LRAC) curve is the lower edge of those curves: for each output, choose the plant with the lowest average cost.

Suppose a bakery can build a small, medium or large plant. These numbers are hypothetical. At 12 batches a day, the ATC is $75 for the small plant, $38 for the medium plant and $42 for the large plant. The medium plant is cheapest, so LRAC at 12 batches is $38. A larger plant is not always cheaper. It only wins at the outputs where its own ATC is lowest.

Choosing the cheapest plant at each output gives LRAC of $40 at 8 batches (medium plant), $36 at 16 batches (large plant) and $48 at 24 batches (large plant). The small plant has one oven and cannot make 24 batches. The slope of LRAC shows returns to scale:
From 8 to 16 batches LRAC falls, which is economies of scale. A possible cause is specialization of workers.
From 16 to 24 batches LRAC rises, which is diseconomies of scale. A possible cause is that a large firm is harder to manage.
If LRAC stays flat, there are constant returns to scale.

When reading the table, compare plants within each output column. Do not pick the lowest number in a plant’s row.

handouts.title: Spend the budget one dollar at a time
handouts.usedIn: Spend the budget one dollar at a time

blocks.text: A student has $24 for the week. Iced coffee costs $4 and a bagel costs $2. The utils below are made-up numbers. Buy one unit at a time: each time, choose the affordable next unit with the highest MU per dollar. When two ratios tie, choose coffee. Stop when the $24 is spent.

blocks.caption: Marginal utility (MU) of each unit, in utils

blocks.hint: Write the order of your purchases and the money spent after each one.
Total utility of my bundle. Show the sum of the marginal utilities.
Total utility of the bundle of 3 coffees and 6 bagels, which also costs $24. Show the sum.
Compare your bundle with your partner's. If they differ, write the step where you chose differently.

handouts.key:
Purchase order and cumulative spending: first bagel, $2; first coffee, $6; second bagel, $8; second coffee, $12; third bagel, $14; third coffee, $18; fourth coffee, $22; fourth bagel, $24. At the tie of 4 utils per dollar, choose coffee as directed.
Coffees in my bundle: 4.
Bagels in my bundle: 4.
Total utility: (40 + 32 + 24 + 16) + (22 + 18 + 14 + 8) = 112 + 62 = 174 utils.
For 3 coffees and 6 bagels: (40 + 32 + 24) + (22 + 18 + 14 + 8 + 6 + 2) = 96 + 70 = 166 utils. The chosen bundle provides 8 more utils.
Partner comparison: Both should obtain 4 coffees and 4 bagels. Look for identification of the first purchase where their sequences differ. Choosing the fourth bagel before the fourth coffee changes the order but yields the same final bundle; the stated tie rule requires coffee first. Common slip: comparing marginal utilities without accounting for prices.

handouts.title: Find and fix the mistake

blocks.text: Each statement below is about the same budget: $24, coffee at $4 and bagels at $2. Each contains exactly one error. Work alone. Find the error and write a corrected version of the statement.

blocks.caption: Marginal utility (MU) of each unit, in utils

blocks.text: Statement 1
The utility-maximizing bundle is the one where the marginal utility of the last coffee equals the marginal utility of the last bagel, and the whole $24 is spent.

blocks.hint: Corrected statement

blocks.text: Statement 2
The first purchase should be a coffee, because the first coffee adds 40 utils and the first bagel adds only 22 utils.

blocks.hint: Corrected statement

blocks.text: Statement 3
Any bundle that spends the whole $24 maximizes utility, so 3 coffees and 6 bagels is as good as 4 coffees and 4 bagels.

blocks.hint: Corrected statement

handouts.key:
Statement 1: Compare marginal utility per dollar, rather than marginal utility alone. Here, 4 coffees and 4 bagels maximize utility and spend $24. The last coffee gives 16 ÷ 4 = 4 utils per dollar; the last bagel gives 8 ÷ 2 = 4 utils per dollar. Their marginal utilities are unequal. Look for both the price adjustment and the budget constraint.
Statement 2: Buy the first bagel first. It gives 22 ÷ 2 = 11 utils per dollar, while the first coffee gives 40 ÷ 4 = 10 utils per dollar. Common slip: treating 40 utils as directly comparable with 22 utils when the prices differ.
Statement 3: Spending the entire budget does not guarantee maximum utility. Both bundles cost $24, but 3 coffees and 6 bagels provide 166 utils, while 4 coffees and 4 bagels provide 174 utils. Replacing the last two bagels with a fourth coffee sacrifices 6 + 2 = 8 utils and gains 16 utils, increasing utility by 8 utils.

handouts.title: The coffee price doubles
handouts.usedIn: The coffee price doubles: where demand comes from

blocks.text: The price of coffee rises from $4 to $8. The budget is still $24 and bagels still cost $2. The marginal utilities in utils are unchanged. Recompute the coffee column at the new price, then find the new utility-maximizing bundle.

blocks.hint: Show that the bundle costs $24 and give its MU per dollar for each good.

blocks.text: With your partner, mark two points on your graph paper, with the price of coffee on the vertical axis and the quantity of coffee on the horizontal axis: the price of $4 with its utility-maximizing quantity, and the price of $8 with its utility-maximizing quantity.

blocks.hint: In one sentence, explain how these two points build the law of demand.

handouts.key:
Coffee MU per dollar at $8, in row order: 40 ÷ 8 = 5; 32 ÷ 8 = 4; 24 ÷ 8 = 3; 16 ÷ 8 = 2; 8 ÷ 8 = 1; 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5.
New bundle: 2 coffees and 4 bagels.
Budget check: (2 × $8) + (4 × $2) = $16 + $8 = $24. Marginal utility per dollar of the last coffee: 32 ÷ 8 = 4. Marginal utility per dollar of the last bagel: 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Total utility is 40 + 32 + 22 + 18 + 14 + 8 = 134 utils.
Graph points, expressed as (quantity of coffee, price of coffee): (4, $4) and (2, $8). Quantity belongs on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis.
Acceptable explanation: Holding income, preferences and the price of bagels constant, raising coffee's price from $4 to $8 reduces the utility-maximizing quantity of coffee from 4 to 2, illustrating the law of demand. Bagel consumption remains 4. Common slips: retaining the old coffee ratios or reversing the graph axes.

handouts.title: Build the cost table

blocks.text: A small bakery has one oven, rented at $60 a day, and hires labor at $5 per labor hour. The numbers are made up. The table gives total cost (TC) in dollars for each daily output Q in batches. Work alone with a calculator.

blocks.hint: Marginal cost at Q = 3. Show the change in TC and the change in Q.
Marginal cost at Q = 4. Show the change in TC and the change in Q.
Average variable cost at Q = 4. Find variable cost first.
Average total cost at Q = 4.
Compare with your partner. Then find average fixed cost at Q = 4 and check that ATC = AFC + AVC.

handouts.key:
Marginal cost at Q = 3: ΔTC ÷ ΔQ = ($150 − $130) ÷ (3 − 2) = $20 per batch.
Marginal cost at Q = 4: ($180 − $150) ÷ (4 − 3) = $30 per batch.
Average variable cost at Q = 4: Fixed cost is $60. Variable cost is $180 − $60 = $120. AVC = $120 ÷ 4 = $30 per batch.
Average total cost at Q = 4: ATC = $180 ÷ 4 = $45 per batch.
Partner comparison and identity: AFC = $60 ÷ 4 = $15 per batch. ATC = AFC + AVC = $15 + $30 = $45 per batch. Look for agreement supported by the calculations. Common slips: dividing total cost by quantity to find marginal cost, or failing to subtract fixed cost before calculating AVC.

handouts.title: Graph the cost curves

blocks.text: Use the completed cost table for the bakery. With a ruler and pencil on graph paper, put quantity (batches, 0 to 6) on the horizontal axis and dollars (0 to 100) on the vertical axis. Plot marginal cost (MC), average variable cost (AVC) and average total cost (ATC) on one graph. Plot each point from the table, then join the points for each curve.

blocks.hint: In one sentence, say where MC crosses ATC on your graph and why it crosses there.

handouts.key:
Plot these (quantity, dollars per batch) coordinates:
MC: (1, 40), (2, 30), (3, 20), (4, 30), (5, 45), (6, 60).
AVC: (1, 40), (2, 35), (3, 30), (4, 30), (5, 33), (6, 37.5).
ATC: (1, 100), (2, 65), (3, 50), (4, 45), (5, 45), (6, 47.5).
Look for labeled axes, the specified scales, distinct labeled curves and points joined in quantity order. No point is plotted at Q = 0.
Acceptable sentence: MC meets ATC at Q = 5 and $45 per batch, where ATC is at its minimum; MC below ATC lowers the average, while MC above ATC raises it.
ATC is $45 at both Q = 4 and Q = 5. The fifth batch costs exactly the previous average, so the average stays unchanged; the sixth batch costs $60, so ATC rises to $47.50. Common slip: forcing MC through a different point instead of plotting the table's values.

handouts.title: Find the long-run average cost

blocks.text: A bakery can build a small, medium or large plant. The numbers are hypothetical. The table gives the average total cost per batch, in dollars, of each plant at three output levels. The small plant has one oven and cannot make 24 batches. For each output, choose the cheapest plant and write the long-run average cost (LRAC).

blocks.caption: Label each step as economies of scale or diseconomies of scale

blocks.hint: Give one possible cause of the change in direction between the two steps.

handouts.key:
8 batches: Medium plant; LRAC = $40 per batch, the minimum of $55, $40 and $52.
16 batches: Large plant; LRAC = $36 per batch, the minimum of $75, $42 and $36.
24 batches: Large plant; LRAC = $48 per batch, the minimum of the feasible costs, $60 and $48.
8 to 16 batches: Economies of scale. LRAC falls from $40 to $36 per batch.
16 to 24 batches: Diseconomies of scale. LRAC rises from $36 to $48 per batch.
Possible cause: Expanding output initially permits greater worker specialization, reducing average cost; further expansion may create coordination and management difficulties that raise average cost. Accept other plausible explanations that distinguish the two effects. These are possible explanations, rather than facts established by the table. Common slips: comparing output levels within one plant instead of choosing the cheapest feasible plant at each output, or treating the unavailable small plant at 24 batches as having zero cost.

segments.title: Problem set due, and should the bakery bake a fifth batch?
segments.description:
The teacher says that Weekly problem sets: Consumer choice and the costs of a firm is due now.
The bakery cost table from last time goes back on the screen. Each student writes whether the bakery should bake a fifth batch if bread sells at $50 a batch, and one sentence why.
Two or three students read out their answer and reason.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: yes. The fifth batch adds $45 to cost and $50 to revenue. Do not confirm the sixth batch yet. Accept any reasoning that compares extra revenue with extra cost. Keep it brisk; the question leads into the profit-maximizing rule.
shown: Prompt: If bread sells at $50 a batch, should the bakery bake a fifth batch? Write one sentence on why.

segments.title: The price taker and the rule MR = MC
segments.description:
The teacher defines perfect competition (many sellers, identical product, free entry) and the price taker. Because every batch sells at the market price, marginal revenue equals price.
The teacher states the rule: keep raising output while marginal revenue is at least marginal cost, and stop when the next unit costs more than it earns.
Using the cost table, each student finds the bakery’s output at a price of $50 and compares with a partner. The teacher then marks the answer on the table.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: 5 batches, since MC is $45 at Q = 5 and $60 at Q = 6. Mistake: stopping at Q = 3 because MC starts to rise there, from $20 to $30; what matters is whether the next batch’s MC is still at or below the $50 price. Link to OpenStax ch. 8.
shown: Steps: Price taker → MR equals price → compare MR with MC → expand while MR is above MC → stop where the next batch costs more than it earns
Prompt: At a price of $50, how many batches does the bakery bake? Use the marginal cost column.

segments.title: Check the rule with profit
segments.description:
With calculators, students find profit at 4, 5 and 6 batches at a price of $50, using the total revenue and total cost on the sheet.
On the handout Bakery cost curves they draw the $50 price line, mark the chosen output and shade the profit rectangle.
Partners compare, and the teacher hears the profit at each quantity.
segments.teacherNotes: Profit: Q = 4, $20; Q = 5, $25; Q = 6, $15. Rectangle: ($50 − $45) × 5 = $25. Prepare copies of Bakery cost curves: a grid with MC, AVC and ATC from last time’s table already plotted. Mistake: using AVC for the rectangle’s height.

segments.title: Profit, break-even or shutdown
segments.description:
Before any explanation, each student writes whether the bakery should still bake if the price falls to $35, and why.
The teacher works prices of $45 and $35 at the profit-maximizing whole-batch output. Price is compared with average total cost for profit or loss, and with average variable cost for the decision to operate.
The teacher defines the break-even point and the shutdown point, and notes that a firm that shuts down still pays its fixed cost.
segments.teacherNotes: P = $45: Q = 5, revenue $225 = cost $225, break-even. P = $35: Q = 4, revenue $140, cost $180, loss $40, less than the $60 fixed cost, and P exceeds AVC of $30, so keep baking. Mistake: shutting down whenever there is a loss.
shown: Table: Price | Whole-batch output (last batch with MC at or below price) | Compare P with ATC | Compare P with AVC | Decision / $50 | 5 | above | above | profit $25 / $45 | 5 | equal | above | break-even / $35 | 4 | below | above | loss, keep baking
Prompt: If the price falls to $35, should the bakery keep baking? Write one sentence on why.

segments.title: Which prices make the bakery shut down?
segments.description:
Students work the case turned around. At a price of $25 they compare the loss from baking with the loss from shutting down.
Using the table and their curve handout, each student then writes the range of prices for profit, for a loss with production continuing, and for shutdown.
Partners compare ranges, and the teacher hears one answer.
segments.teacherNotes: At $25: Q = 3, revenue $75, cost $150, loss $75, against $60 if closed, so shut down. Ranges: above $45 profit; at $45 break even; above $30 and below $45 make a loss but keep baking; below $30 shut down. At $30, producing three or four batches and shutting down all give a $60 loss, so the firm is indifferent. Mistake: using the ATC minimum as the shutdown price.

segments.title: Break
segments.description:
Students take a break.
The teacher leaves the bakery cost table on the screen for the next segment.
segments.teacherNotes: Ask students to keep their curve handout and ruler for the monopoly graph.

segments.title: The monopolist and its marginal revenue
segments.description:
The teacher defines monopoly and barriers to entry, and explains that the monopolist faces the whole market demand curve. To sell more, it must cut the price on every unit.
Before the table is explained, each student writes whether marginal revenue from the second batch is above or below its $75 price, and why.
Students compute total revenue and marginal revenue for 1, 2 and 3 batches, then the teacher completes the rest of the rows.
segments.teacherNotes: TR: 85, 150, 195, 220, 225, 210. MR: 85, 65, 45, 25, 5, −15. The second batch earns $75 but the first now sells for $75 instead of $85, so MR is $65. Mistake: treating price as marginal revenue. Refer to OpenStax ch. 9.
shown: Prompt: Will marginal revenue from the second batch be above or below its $75 price? Write one sentence on why.

segments.title: The monopolist chooses
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “The monopolist's table”.
The full table is on the sheet with total revenue, marginal revenue, marginal cost and total cost. Students compare MR with MC row by row and pick the output.
They read the price from the demand column and compute profit at that output. They check profit at one batch more and one batch fewer.
Partners compare quantity, price and profit, and the teacher hears them.
segments.teacherNotes: Q = 3: MR $45 exceeds MC $20, but at Q = 4 MR $25 is below MC $30. Price $65, profit $195 − $150 = $45. Q = 2: $20; Q = 4: $40. Mistake: reading the price off the MR column.

segments.title: Monopoly against competition
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Monopoly against the competitive benchmark”.
Suppose, as a hypothetical assumption, that a competitive industry’s aggregate total costs and marginal costs match the bakery table on the sheet, including the $60 fixed cost. Students find the output and price where the demand price equals marginal cost, the competitive benchmark.
In pairs they write one sentence comparing price, output and profit under the monopolist and the benchmark, and why the monopolist holds output back.
Two pairs are heard, and the teacher closes on the pattern. The teacher explains that positive economic profit attracts entry under perfect competition, increasing market supply and lowering price until economic profit is zero in long-run equilibrium; barriers to entry can allow monopoly profit to persist.
segments.teacherNotes: Benchmark under the assumed industry costs: Q = 5, price $45 = MC, profit 0. Monopoly: Q = 3, price $65, profit $45. At Q = 3 MR $45 exceeds MC $20; at Q = 4 MR $25 is below MC $30. Buyers of batches 4 and 5 are priced out. Mention antitrust, OpenStax ch. 11, in one sentence.

segments.title: Individual check: two new cases
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Two new cases”.
Working alone with a calculator, each student solves two new cases on the sheet. The first is a price taker at a new price and the second is a monopolist with new numbers.
The teacher gives the answers at the end, and students mark their own work.
segments.teacherNotes:
Practice only, with no grade.
(a) Price $40: Q = 4, revenue $160, cost $180, loss $20; P exceeds AVC of $30, so keep baking.
(b) MR: 70, 50, 30, 10, with MC $25. Q = 3, price $50, TR $150, TC $40 + 3 × $25 = $115, profit $35.

segments.title: Homework and next time
segments.description:
The teacher sets Weekly problem sets, which count for 30% of the course grade and are due at the start of next time. The practice quiz on today’s lesson is for after class and counts toward no grade.
The teacher previews how next time students will use demand, supply and marginal analysis to examine externalities, public goods and government responses.
Before next time, students read OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e, ch. 12 (Environmental Protection and Negative Externalities) and ch. 13 (Positive Externalities and Public Goods).
Before students leave, tell them that next time ends with a review for the Final exam, which is sat afterwards on a day you announce.

keyIdeas: A price taker cannot change the market price, so each extra batch it sells adds the same revenue: marginal revenue equals price. With continuously divisible output, it maximizes profit where marginal revenue equals rising marginal cost, so P = MC. With whole batches, compare total profits and stop before an additional batch reduces profit.

At that output, compare price with average total cost to find profit, break-even or loss. Compare price with average variable cost to decide whether to keep producing or shut down. A firm that shuts down loses only its fixed cost.

A monopolist faces the whole market demand curve. To sell one more unit it must cut the price on every unit, so its marginal revenue is below its price. With continuously divisible output, it chooses output where MR = MC, then reads the price from the demand curve. With whole batches, it compares total profits and stops before an additional batch reduces profit.
Compared with competition, a monopoly produces less and charges more, and it can keep a profit. A competitive firm’s long-run profit is driven to zero by entry.

vocabulary.definition: A market with many sellers of an identical product and free entry and exit, so no seller can affect the price.
A firm that sells at the market price and cannot change it by changing its own output.
The change in total revenue from selling one more unit; for a price taker it equals the price.
The price at which price equals average total cost at the chosen output, so profit is zero.
The price at the minimum of average variable cost; below it a firm loses less by producing nothing in the short run.
A market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes.
Anything that keeps other firms from entering a market, such as a legal license or control of a key resource.

study.overview:
This guide covers one rule and what it tells us about two kinds of firm. A firm maximizes profit by adding output while the extra revenue is at least the extra cost, and stopping when the next unit costs more than it earns. A price taker and a monopolist both follow this rule, but they face different revenue. We use one running example, a bakery selling batches of bread with a fixed cost of $60. The bakery’s costs are:

Batches (Q) | Total cost | Marginal cost | Average variable cost | Average total cost
0 | $60 | – | – | –
1 | $100 | $40 | $40 | $100
2 | $130 | $30 | $35 | $65
3 | $150 | $20 | $30 | $50
4 | $180 | $30 | $30 | $45
5 | $225 | $45 | $33 | $45
6 | $285 | $60 | $37.50 | $47.50

For background, see the chapters on perfect competition and on monopoly in OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics 3e.

points.heading: A price taker sets output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
points.explanation:
Under perfect competition there are many sellers, the product is identical, and entry is free. One seller cannot change the market price, so every extra batch adds the same revenue. Marginal revenue (MR) equals price. The rule is to keep raising output while MR is at least marginal cost (MC), and stop when the next batch costs more than it earns. With continuously divisible output this gives P = MC. With whole batches, compare total profits and stop before an extra batch reduces profit.

Example: the bakery sells bread at $50 a batch. The fifth batch adds $45 to cost (MC) and $50 to revenue, so baking it pays. The sixth batch adds $60 to cost and $50 to revenue, so it does not. The bakery bakes 5 batches. Check with profit (total revenue minus total cost): 4 batches give $200 − $180 = $20, 5 batches give $250 − $225 = $25, and 6 batches give $300 − $285 = $15. On a graph, the profit rectangle has height price minus average total cost, ($50 − $45), and width equal to output, 5. Its area is $25. Use ATC for the height, not AVC. A common error is to stop at 3 batches because MC starts rising after the third batch, from $20 to $30. What matters is the last batch whose MC is at or below the price.

points.heading: Compare price with ATC for profit and with AVC for shutdown
points.explanation:
After finding the output where MR = MC, ask two separate questions. First, is the firm making money? Compare price with average total cost (ATC). Price above ATC means profit, equal means break-even, below means loss. Second, should it keep producing? Compare price with average variable cost (AVC). If price covers AVC, producing loses less than closing, because closing still costs the whole fixed cost. If price is below AVC, shut down and lose only the fixed cost.

Example with the bakery table:
$45: output is 5 batches, revenue $225, cost $225. Price equals ATC, so the bakery breaks even.
$35: output is 4 batches, revenue $140, cost $180, loss $40. The loss is below the $60 fixed cost, and the price exceeds AVC of $30, so it keeps baking.
$25: output is 3 batches, revenue $75, cost $150, loss $75. That is worse than the $60 lost by closing, so it shuts down.

Price ranges: above $45 is profit; $45 is break-even; between $30 and $45 is a loss but keep baking; below $30 means shut down. At exactly $30 the loss is $60 whether it bakes 3 batches, 4 batches or none, so the bakery is indifferent. Two mistakes to avoid: shutting down whenever there is a loss, and treating the minimum of ATC ($45) as the shutdown price. The shutdown point is the minimum of AVC ($30).

points.heading: A monopolist’s marginal revenue is below its price
points.explanation:
A monopoly is the only seller, protected by barriers to entry. It faces the whole market demand curve, so to sell one more unit it must cut the price on every unit. Marginal revenue is therefore below price. With continuously divisible output the monopolist picks the output where MR = MC, then reads its price from the demand curve, not from the MR column. With whole batches, compare total profits and stop before an extra batch reduces profit.

Example: the bakery is now the only seller, with the same costs as above.

Batches | Price | Total revenue | Marginal revenue | Marginal cost
1 | $85 | $85 | $85 | $40
2 | $75 | $150 | $65 | $30
3 | $65 | $195 | $45 | $20
4 | $55 | $220 | $25 | $30
5 | $45 | $225 | $5 | $45
6 | $35 | $210 | −$15 | $60

The second batch sells for $75, but the first batch now also sells for $75 instead of $85. The net gain is $75 − $10 = $65, which is below the $75 price. At 3 batches MR of $45 exceeds MC of $20. At 4 batches MR of $25 is below MC of $30. So the monopolist produces 3 batches and charges $65. Profit is $195 − $150 = $45. Check the neighbors: 2 batches give $150 − $130 = $20 and 4 batches give $220 − $180 = $40. Both are lower than $45.

points.heading: Monopoly produces less and charges more than competition
points.explanation:
To compare, we need a competitive benchmark: the output and price where the demand price equals marginal cost. Suppose, as a hypothetical assumption, that a competitive industry’s total and marginal costs match the bakery table, including the $60 fixed cost. Using the same demand as the monopoly example, the benchmark is 5 batches at $45, where price equals MC of $45. Profit there is $225 − $225 = 0. The monopolist produces 3 batches at $65 and earns $45.

The monopolist holds output back because selling more means cutting the price on all units it sells, and by the fourth batch the extra revenue ($25) is below the extra cost ($30). Buyers of the fourth and fifth batches, who would pay $55 and $45, are priced out, even though they would pay at least the cost of making their batch. So compared with competition, a monopoly produces less and charges more.

The profit also differs over time. Under perfect competition, positive economic profit attracts entry. Market supply rises, the price falls, and economic profit is driven to zero in long-run equilibrium. Barriers to entry can let monopoly profit last. This is why governments use antitrust policy, covered in the OpenStax chapter on monopoly and antitrust.

keyIdeas: A negative externality is a cost that falls on people outside a transaction. The social cost of a good is its private cost plus that external cost, so the market output is larger than the output that is best for society.

A per-unit tax equal to the external cost makes the producer face the social cost and moves output to the socially best quantity. A subsidy equal to the external benefit does the same for a positive externality.

Goods are classified by two tests: rival or nonrival, and excludable or nonexcludable. A public good is nonrival and nonexcludable, so people can free ride and private markets supply too little of it.
Every tool from earlier in the course (the PPF, supply and demand, elasticity, marginal utility per dollar, MR = MC, monopoly pricing) is a way of comparing marginal benefit with marginal cost.

vocabulary.definition: A cost or benefit of a transaction that falls on people who are not part of it.
An externality that harms outsiders, so the social cost of the good is higher than its private cost.
An externality that benefits outsiders, so the social benefit of the good is higher than its private benefit.
The private cost of producing a good plus the external cost it imposes on others.
A good is rival if one person’s use of it leaves less for others.
A good is excludable if people who do not pay can be kept from using it.
A good that is nonrival and nonexcludable, such as national defense.
A person who benefits from a good without paying for it, leaving others to bear the cost.

study.overview: This lesson asked one question in several settings: when does a market choose the wrong quantity, and what can a government do about it? A market uses only the costs and benefits that buyers and sellers themselves face. When a cost or benefit falls on someone else, the quantity traded is too high or too low for society. When a good is nonrival and nonexcludable, private markets supply too little of it. The same logic ties the whole course together. The PPF, supply and demand, elasticity, marginal utility per dollar, MR = MC and monopoly pricing each compare marginal benefit with marginal cost. The final exam is on what has been taught so far, so use this idea to check your review. For each topic, ask which marginal benefit and which marginal cost are being compared.

points.heading: A negative externality is a gap between private and social cost
points.explanation:
An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on people outside the transaction. With a negative externality, the social marginal cost of a good equals the private marginal cost plus the external cost per unit. Sellers respond only to their private cost, so the market output is larger than the output that is best for society.

Example (the numbers are invented). A paper mill sells paper, and each ton puts $20 of cost on a fishing town downstream.

Tons | Buyers’ price per ton | Private marginal cost | Social marginal cost
1 | $70 | $10 | $30
2 | $60 | $20 | $40
3 | $50 | $30 | $50
4 | $40 | $40 | $60
5 | $30 | $50 | $70
6 | $20 | $60 | $80

The market settles at 4 tons and $40, where the buyers’ price equals the mill’s private marginal cost. The best output is 3 tons, where the buyers’ price equals social marginal cost at $50. The fourth ton costs society $60 and is worth only $40 to buyers, so it is a net loss of $20. A common mistake is to stop at 4 tons because price equals private cost. The $20 is not the mill’s cost. It is paid by others, so it never enters the mill’s decision.

points.heading: A tax or a subsidy makes the decision-maker face the full cost or benefit
points.explanation:
A per-unit tax equal to the external cost raises the producer’s marginal cost to the social marginal cost. Output then falls to the socially best quantity. A subsidy equal to the external benefit does the same job when the outside effect is a benefit. A tax does not remove all pollution. It moves output to the point where the last unit is worth what it costs society. Other responses include a cap on output and tradable pollution permits.

Tax example. Put a $20 tax on each ton the mill sells. The mill’s cost per ton becomes $30, $40, $50, $60 and so on. Now 3 tons trade. Buyers pay $50, the mill keeps $30 per ton after the tax, and the tax raises 3 × $20 = $60. Buyers pay $10 more than the untaxed $40 and the mill keeps $10 less, so here they share the $20 equally.

Subsidy example (invented numbers). A flu shot costs $25. The private benefit to the buyer of shots 1 to 6 is $50, $40, $30, $20, $10 and $0. Each shot also protects others, a benefit worth $20. Social benefit is therefore $70, $60, $50, $40, $30 and $20.

Without a subsidy, buyers take 3 shots, because the third is worth $30 to them, which is at least $25, and the fourth is worth only $20. The best quantity is 5, because the fifth shot is worth $30 to society against a cost of $25, and the sixth is worth $20. A $20 subsidy cuts the buyer’s net cost to $5, so buyers take 5 shots. The subsidy costs the government 5 × $20 = $100. The mistake to avoid is taxing here. A positive externality calls for a subsidy.

points.heading: Classify goods with two tests: rival and excludable
points.explanation:
A good is rival if one person’s use leaves less for others. It is excludable if nonpayers can be kept from using it. Placing a good in the two-by-two table tells you how a private market will treat it.

Excludable and rival: a hamburger. This is a private good.
Excludable and nonrival: a streaming service subscription.
Nonexcludable and rival: fish in the open ocean. This is a common resource.
Nonexcludable and nonrival: national defense and a tornado warning siren. These are public goods.

A public good is nonrival and nonexcludable. Whether the government provides a good is not the test. Public schools are provided by government, but they are rival (a classroom seat is used up) and excludable (a school can limit enrollment), so they are not public goods.

points.heading: Free riding explains why private markets undersupply public goods
points.explanation:
If people cannot be excluded, each person can enjoy the good without paying. This is the free rider problem. Each person hopes others will pay, so voluntary payment falls short.

Example (invented numbers). A town of 100 households is deciding on a fireworks display that costs $5,000. Every household would pay up to $80 to see it, so the total value is 100 × $80 = $8,000. The display is worth providing, because $8,000 exceeds $5,000. Everyone in town can see it, and one household watching takes nothing from another’s view, so the display is nonrival and nonexcludable. If the council asks for voluntary contributions, each household can reason that it will see the show whether or not it pays. Contributions may then fall below $5,000 and the show may not happen.

A sensible response is tax-funded provision. Charging $50 per household would raise the $5,000, and each household values the show at $80. Admission fees would not work well, because there is no way to keep nonpayers from seeing fireworks over the lake.

blocks.text: Suppose a town of 100 households is deciding whether to put on a fireworks display over the lake (the numbers are invented). The display costs $5,000. Every household would pay up to $80 to see it. The fireworks can be seen from every home in town, and one household watching does not take anything away from another household's view. The town council asks households to contribute voluntarily.
Write an answer to each question before any group speaks.
Is the display worth providing? Use the numbers in your answer.

blocks.hint: Your group's answer.

blocks.text: Why might voluntary contributions fall short of what the display costs?

blocks.hint: Your group's answer.

blocks.text: Which response by the town would your group choose, and why?

blocks.hint: Your group's answer.

handouts.key:
Worth providing: yes. Total willingness to pay = 100 × $80 = $8,000. This exceeds the $5,000 cost by $3,000. Look for a comparison of total benefit with total cost.
Voluntary contributions: households can watch without paying, and one household’s viewing does not reduce another’s. Each household has an incentive to let others pay. Contributions may therefore fall short even though total willingness to pay exceeds cost. Look for the free rider problem; do not require a claim that contributions must be zero.
Government response: tax-funded provision is a well-supported choice. An equal tax would be $5,000 ÷ 100 = $50 per household, below each household’s $80 willingness to pay. Accept another feasible response supported by an explanation of how it finances the display and addresses free riding. An admission-fee proposal must explain how nonpayers could be excluded despite visibility from every home.
Common slips: comparing one household’s $80 benefit with the entire $5,000 cost; assuming voluntary payment necessarily reflects the display’s full value; assuming an admission fee alone prevents free riding.

blocks.text: Work all six problems with a calculator. Write every answer with the reason for it. All numbers are invented.
Problem 1

A farm can produce wheat and tractors. Producing the first 10 tractors costs 20 tons of wheat. Producing the next 10 tractors costs a further 40 tons of wheat. Find the opportunity cost of one tractor in each block of 10, and say what this tells you about the shape of the production possibilities frontier.

blocks.hint: Opportunity cost in each block, and what it shows.

blocks.text: Problem 2

When the price of a good falls from $12 to $8, the quantity demanded rises from 40 to 60. Use the midpoint method to find the price elasticity of demand, and say whether demand is elastic, inelastic or unit elastic. Then find total revenue at each price and say what happens to it.

blocks.hint: Percentage changes, elasticity, classification, and total revenue at $12 and at $8.

blocks.text: Problem 3

Pizza is a normal good. Suppose incomes rise and, at the same time, the price of cheese, an input in making pizza, falls. Use demand and supply to say what happens to the equilibrium quantity and the equilibrium price of pizza. For each of the two, say whether it rises, falls or cannot be told, and why.

blocks.hint: Which curve shifts, in which direction, and the effect on quantity and on price.

blocks.text: Problem 4

A firm in a perfectly competitive market sells 10 units at a market price of $8. At that output its average total cost is $12 and its average variable cost is $6. Find the firm's profit or loss. Should it keep producing in the short run or shut down?

blocks.hint: Profit or loss, and your decision with its reason.

blocks.text: Problem 5

A consumer buys coffee at $5 a cup and bagels at $3 each. The last cup of coffee gives 20 utils and the last bagel gives 15 utils. Calculate the marginal utility per dollar for each good. Is the consumer maximizing utility? If not, how should spending change?

blocks.hint: Marginal utility per dollar for each good, and your advice.

blocks.text: Problem 6
A monopolist can sell 1 unit at a price of $10, or 2 units at a price of $9 each. Find the marginal revenue of the second unit.

blocks.hint: Total revenue at 1 and at 2 units, and marginal revenue.

handouts.key:
Problem 1: First block: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 tons of wheat per tractor. Next block: 40 ÷ 10 = 4 tons of wheat per tractor. Opportunity cost increases. With tractors on the horizontal axis and wheat on the vertical axis, the PPF becomes steeper as tractor production rises, consistent with a PPF bowed outward from the origin. Common slip: reporting 20 and 40 tons as the cost of one tractor.

Problem 2: Average quantity = (40 + 60) ÷ 2 = 50. Quantity change = 20 ÷ 50 = 40%. Average price = ($12 + $8) ÷ 2 = $10. Price change = −$4 ÷ $10 = −40%. Price elasticity of demand = 40% ÷ −40% = −1; its absolute value is 1, so demand is unit elastic over this interval. Revenue at $12 = $12 × 40 = $480. Revenue at $8 = $8 × 60 = $480. Revenue is unchanged. Common slips: using starting values instead of midpoint values; interpreting a negative elasticity as inelastic demand.

Problem 3: Higher incomes shift demand right because pizza is a normal good. Cheaper cheese lowers production costs and shifts supply right. Both shifts increase equilibrium quantity, so quantity rises. Higher demand pushes price up; higher supply pushes price down. The net price change cannot be determined without the relative sizes of the shifts. Common slip: treating an input-price change as a movement along the supply curve.

Problem 4: Total revenue = $8 × 10 = $80. Total cost = $12 × 10 = $120. Profit = $80 − $120 = −$40: a $40 loss. Variable cost = $6 × 10 = $60. Fixed cost = $120 − $60 = $60. Producing covers variable cost and contributes $20 toward fixed cost. Continue producing in the short run rather than shut down: the $40 operating loss is smaller than the $60 loss from shutting down. Common slip: recommending shutdown solely because price is below average total cost.

Problem 5: Coffee: 20 ÷ $5 = 4 utils per dollar. Bagels: 15 ÷ $3 = 5 utils per dollar. The allocation does not satisfy the equal-marginal-utility-per-dollar condition for an interior optimum. Shift spending toward bagels and away from coffee. With diminishing marginal utility and divisible purchases, adjustment continues until marginal utility per dollar is equal across the goods. Common slip: comparing 20 utils with 15 utils without accounting for prices.

Problem 6: Revenue from 1 unit = 1 × $10 = $10. Revenue from 2 units = 2 × $9 = $18. Marginal revenue of the second unit = $18 − $10 = $8. Common slip: giving $9 and ignoring the $1 reduction in revenue on the first unit.

t_b7102fcd1878.explanation: The economy gives up 12 baskets to produce 2 more tons of vegetables. Divide 12 by 2 to get 6 baskets per additional ton.

Plot (0, 40), (1, 3), (2, 7), and (3, 12), then connect adjacent points.
Plot (0, 40), (1, 43), (2, 50), and (3, 62), then connect adjacent points.
